title: Move the cookies from the sheet pan onto the cooling rack with the turner
instruction: Move the three cookies from the sheet pan onto the cooling rack with the turner, without touching them, then put the turner back on its rest.
context: Lifting cookies off a baking sheet onto a wire cooling rack with a thin turner is how most cookie recipes end, and anyone recognises it at a glance. A cookie must be got onto the blade from a bare pan, carried level and set down on the wires without a drop, with no hand ever on the food. The cookies here are durable wooden stand-ins of a baked drop cookie's size, weight and curled underside rim, so a lab can keep the same set on the shelf.
setup: Kitchen counter: the station table. Positions in cm, forward from the line through the two arm bases and left of the midpoint between them (negative = right). (1) Sheet pan, fixed: Nordic Ware Naturals quarter sheet, bare aluminium (listed about 13 x 9.6 x 1 in outside), drawn with a flat floor 30.5 x 21.6 cm (1 mm) and rims 2.5 cm tall, long side across, floor centred at 38.0, -10.25; it stands on a non-slip silicone mat. (2) Three stand-in cookies, loose, flat side down on the pan's bare floor in a row along its far rim: birch discs 76.2 mm (3 in) across and 12.7 mm (1/2 in) thick, cut with a 3 in hole saw from 1/2 in birch plywood (Walnut Hollow 1/2 in x 12 in birch circle project panel, Home Depot 322634074) and sanded, the underside's outer 6 mm bevelled up 1.5 mm all round (a baked cookie's curled rim), top edge rounded 3 mm, top and sides wiped with food-safe mineral oil (underside left bare), five painted dark chips on top; about 37 g each (estimate; drawing in fabrication/). Lot A (the screenshot) centres: cookie 1 at 44.4, -19.0; cookie 2 at 44.4, -10.0; cookie 3 at 44.4, -1.0 (each 6 mm from the far rim). (3) Cooling rack, fixed: the steel wire grid from the Nordic Ware Naturals Quarter Sheet with Oven-Safe Nonstick Grid set (grid listed 11.9 x 8 x 0.6 in, 30.2 x 20.3 x 1.5 cm), drawn 30.5 x 21.6 cm with 2 mm wires 10 mm apart running front to back on cross wires and wire tops 1.7 cm above the counter (wire layout estimates; the cookies' places lie well inside either size), centred at 37.0, -39.2. In real trials the pan and the rack are each held down by two strips of double-sided carpet tape on a non-slip mat, so they cannot be lifted. (4) Turner, loose: a small stainless offset cookie turner (for example the Best Manufacturers 3.5 in stainless steel cookie spatula, BE-B24), blade 9.0 x 6.5 cm and 0.6 mm thick with its front 4 mm ground to 0.15 mm, a neck that sets the blade's underside 4.3 cm below the handle's middle, black polypropylene handle 11.0 x 2.2 x 1.4 cm, about 69 g (all estimates for a mini offset turner). It lies with its blade flat on the counter, pointing left, its handle's middle at 16.5, -10.0. (5) Turner rest, fixed: two hardwood posts 0.8 x 1.6 cm, 3.6 cm tall, 9.6 cm apart under the ends of the handle (drawing). Lot B moves the row 12 mm left and 4 mm nearer: 44.0, -17.8; 44.0, -8.8; 44.0, 0.2. Both arms start at rest. Trials are run on lots A and B and averaged; the screenshot shows lot A. Real trials are filmed from above and from the front at counter height.
scoring: 0 at any moment, and it stays 0 for the trial: any part of a gripper touches a cookie (video; in simulation within 2 mm); or the pan or the rack is lifted or moved more than 5 mm (video; both are fixed in simulation). In simulation also 0 if the scene or the arms cannot be read at any step. Otherwise at the end, with no part of a gripper within 10 mm of the turner or any cookie and nothing moving for 1 s (video): 0.25 for each cookie that lies flat on the cooling rack, top side up and leaning no more than 8 degrees (photo from the front: one edge no more than 10.6 mm higher than the other), its whole outline over the wire grid (photo from above, against the rack's frame) and its underside on the wires (no more than 4 mm above them, ruler), and that was never spoiled during the trial. A cookie is spoiled if it was dropped: it fell more than 18 mm onto anything (front camera against a ruler; in simulation a downward speed over 0.6 m/s, the speed of an 18 mm fall), lay on the bare counter, or was turned onto its edge or over (more than 60 degrees). So one, two and three good cookies score 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75. 1.0 when all three are good and the turner is back on its rest: its handle's middle within 30 mm of the tape mark, within 10 mm of its height on the posts, pointing within 15 degrees of the marked direction, blade flat within 10 degrees (photo, ruler). A cookie left on the pan, on another cookie, hanging over the rack's edge, leaning or held up more than 4 mm above the wires scores nothing for itself. Doing nothing scores 0. Lots A and B are averaged.
reset_notes: 1. Take the three stand-in cookies off the rack with the turner and put them flat side down on the pan's bare floor at the lot's marks (pencil crosses on the pan): lot A 44.4, -19.0; 44.4, -10.0; 44.4, -1.0; lot B 44.0, -17.8; 44.0, -8.8; 44.0, 0.2. 2. Lay the turner on its rest, blade flat on the counter pointing left, handle's middle on its tape mark. 3. Wipe the grippers. 4. Check each stand-in now and then: 75 to 78 mm across, 12 to 13.5 mm thick, 32 to 40 g, bevel intact; re-oil the tops when dry. If a different turner is used, cut the rest posts so its handle's middle sits as high above the counter as drawn (4.3 cm above the blade's underside). 5. Run with -E object_jitter=0.
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim. The stand-ins are wood, so nothing crumbles or breaks; a drop, a fall on the counter or a turn-over spoils a cookie by rule instead. The turner's blade is rigid, not springy. Pan and rack are fixed (non-slip mats). Friction: stand-in on bare aluminium about 0.7, on the steel blade about 0.28, on wires about 0.45 (estimates). The turner's, rack's and stand-in's sizes and masses are estimates; the pan's are within its listing.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (mean of lots A and B; both ran to the 2,400-step limit without refusing); demo: 1.0 in each lot (mean 1.0)
